newsitem.title: SPAIN: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE TIGHTLIPPED OVER 1998 PLANS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE TIGHTLIPPED OVER 1998 PLANS.

text.p: Speculation over his future with Williams followed Jacques Villeneuve's commanding victory in the Spanish Grand Prix.
Paddock sources indicated he had not yet signed to remain with the Williams team for 1998 despite indications earlier in the season that he was staying.
Asked about his plans for next season, Villeneuve would say only: "Everything is fine."
It should be fine if he can open a decisive lead in the world drivers' championship in his home Canadian Grand Prix next month at the track named after his father Gilles.
Another win would almost certainly improve his bargaining position when his pay talks with Williams begin in earnest in August, assuming that the team take up their option on his services.
Villeneuve, who returned to form at the Circuit de Catalunya on Sunday after two successive non-scoring races, now has 30 points in the title race and a lead of three over Michael Schumacher.
But Ferrari, with 41 points, still retain a one-point advantage over Williams in the teams' title race thanks to their superior consistency over the opening six races of the 17-race calendar.

Schumacher struggled in fourth in his Ferrari and admitted it was all he had hoped for because of his car's relative lack of performance on the sweeping Spanish track when both Eddie Irvine, in the second Ferrari, and Heinz-Harald Frentzen, in the second Williams, failed to score.
Ferrari, however, are the only team to have scored points in every race this year while Williams, in complete contrast to their rivals, have scored points only with victories.
For Williams, this '10 or bust' trend has meant that Frentzen has contributed only 10 points, or one result, from his six outings
"Not really satisfactory," was the pithy verdict on this contribution from his team boss Frank Williams.

Frentzen was puzzling over the tyre-wear problems which let him down along with several other Goodyear-clad drivers on a day when Olivier Panis upset the odds again by finishing second in his Bridgestone-tyred Prost car, after starting from 12th on the grid.
Schumacher, David Coulthard in a McLaren and Gerhard Berger in a Benetton all complained about the inconsistency and high-wear of their Goodyear tyres.
